t.4.3.1: Having understood the words of the great-souled Sugrīva, Hanumān leapt from Mount Ṛśyamūka to where the two Rāghavas were.
t.4.3.2: Having gone there, the mighty Hanumān, the best of monkeys, whose valor was true, approached the two of them with gentle words.
t.4.3.3: Casting off his own form, the monkey took the guise of a mendicant; he addressed those two heroes and praised them in a fitting manner.
t.4.3.4: You two, resembling royal sages and gods, ascetics firm in your vows, of excellent complexion, how have you come to this region?
t.4.3.5: The two of them, frightening the herds of deer and the other creatures roaming the forest, gazed all around at the trees growing on the banks of the Pampā.
t.4.3.6: Who are you two, swift and mighty, steadfast, shining like gold and clad in bark garments, gracing this river of auspicious waters with your presence?
t.4.3.7: You two heroes, with the gaze of lions and with valour surpassing even the might of lions, grasp in your mighty arms bows that resemble the bow of Śakra.
t.4.3.8: Glorious and endowed with beauty, with the valor of the finest of bulls, with arms like an elephant's trunk, radiant, the two are bulls among men.
t.4.3.9: This lord of mountains is illumined by the radiance of you two. Worthy of kingship and resembling the immortals, how is it that you have come here to this region?
t.4.3.10: Two heroes with eyes like lotus petals, wearing coils of matted hair, two heroes alike to one another, as though come down from the world of the gods.
t.4.3.11: You two broad-chested heroes, men with the forms of gods, seem like the moon and the sun arrived upon the earth as if by chance.
t.4.3.12: You two, lion-shouldered and of great strength, are like a pair of bulls in rut; your arms, long and well-rounded like the finest iron bars, are worthy of being adorned with every ornament, so why are they not adorned?
t.4.3.13: I deem you both fit to protect this entire earth, with its oceans and forests, adorned by the Vindhya and Meru mountains.
t.4.3.14: And these two bows of yours, wondrous and smooth, with their brilliant coatings, shine like the two thunderbolts of Indra adorned with gold.
t.4.3.15: And your quivers, lovely to behold, are filled with sharpened arrows, terrible and life-ending, like blazing serpents.
t.4.3.16: These two swords, of great size and broad, adorned with refined gold, shine forth like a pair of serpents that have cast off their sloughs.
t.4.3.17: Why do you two not speak to me in reply, when I am addressing you in this way?
t.4.3.18: There is a certain leader of the monkey troops, a righteous-souled hero named Sugrīva, who, wronged by his brother, wanders the world in sorrow.
t.4.3.19: I, a monkey named Hanumān, have come here, sent by that great-souled Sugrīva, the king of the foremost among the monkeys.
t.4.3.20: The righteous Sugrīva desires friendship with you two. Take me, the monkey, son of the Wind, as one known to be his minister.
t.4.3.21: Disguised in the form of a mendicant, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to Sugrīva, I have come here from Ṛśyamūka, one who goes wherever he wishes and assumes any form at will.
t.4.3.22: Having thus spoken to those two heroes, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who understood speech well, Hanumān, skilled in speech, said nothing further.
t.4.3.23: Having heard these words of his, the glorious Rāma, his face beaming with joy, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, his brother standing at his side.
t.4.3.24: This is the minister of the great-souled Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, and he has come into my presence just as I was longing for that very Sugrīva.
t.4.3.25: O Saumitri, speak with sweet words to this monkey, Sugrīva's minister, who is skilled in speech, full of affection, and a subduer of foes.
